title: Drowning
summary: Someone rescued from water: rescue safely, CPR with breaths first, no abdominal thrusts, warm them, and observe or evacuate even if they seem fine.

steps.text: Do not become a second casualty. Reach with a pole or branch, throw a rope or anything that floats, or use a boat. Go into the water only if you are trained.
steps.detail:
WMS 2024: untrained rescuers should only reach, throw or row; only trained rescuers should enter the water. MedlinePlus: do not go into rough water or onto ice; reach with your arm or an object if you can.

Never try chest compressions in the water (WMS). Rescue breaths in the water are only for trained rescuers with suitable equipment, in safe water, when the shore is far away (WMS); otherwise get them out first.

Keep the casualty as level as you can when lifting them out (WMS hypothermia guideline: horizontal, especially from cold water).

steps.text: Once out of the water, check: do they respond? Are they breathing normally?
steps.detail: Gasping or occasional breaths are not normal breathing. If you are not sure, treat it as not breathing normally.

ask.q: Are they unresponsive and not breathing normally?

steps.text: Start CPR with rescue breaths now: use the CPR, adult protocol (or CPR, child or CPR, infant). If you are trained, you may give breaths first.
steps.detail:
Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

Breaths matter most after drowning, because the heart stopped from lack of oxygen (AHA 2025, WMS). AHA 2025: give CPR with breaths (Class 1). A trained rescuer may start with breaths before compressions, but breaths should not delay compressions. If you are untrained or cannot give breaths, compression-only CPR is still reasonable (AHA); WMS says it is likely to help little and should be limited to people not trained in rescue breathing.

AED: start CPR with breaths before putting the AED on (AHA 2025). Do not delay breathing for them to fetch or apply an AED; AEDs are safe in wet places and on boats (WMS).

Neck injury is rare after drowning unless they dived into shallow water or there was another clear injury (WMS, MedlinePlus). Do not let a possible neck injury stop you giving breaths; keep the head and neck in line as far as you can (MedlinePlus).

Cold water: they may also be hypothermic. The Hypothermia protocol explains how CPR differs in a very cold person; keep them insulated from the ground.

When to stop (WMS 2024): stopping may be reasonable if they were under water for more than 30 minutes in water warmer than about 43°F (6°C), more than 90 minutes in colder water, or after 25 minutes of continuous CPR. If they are very cold, see the Hypothermia protocol before stopping: it advises continuing CPR in a very cold person. Otherwise stop when the CPR protocol says to.

steps.text: Do not push on the belly to get water out. If they vomit, turn them onto their side so it drains, clear vomit you can see from the mouth, then roll them back and continue CPR.
steps.warn: No abdominal thrusts to expel water.
steps.detail:
Abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich manoeuvre) are not recommended for drowning at any time (WMS 2024). They can make an unconscious person vomit and breathe it in (MedlinePlus).

Keep doing CPR. Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth and remove any object you can see. Never do blind finger sweeps.

Vomiting is common. Turning the person on their side lets vomit run out of the mouth instead of into the lungs (Recovery position protocol).

If they start breathing normally, lie them on their side (Recovery position protocol), keep them warm, and evacuate.

steps.text: Breathing: if they dived into shallow water or hit their head, keep the head and neck in line and use the Neck or back (spine) injury protocol. Otherwise, if not fully awake, lie them on their side.
steps.detail:
Once breathing starts, they may cough and struggle to breathe; reassure them (MedlinePlus). Keep them calm and still (MedlinePlus).

WMS: take care with anyone who is not fully alert or is vomiting, because they can breathe vomit into the lungs. The side position lets it drain.

Neck injury is rare unless they dived into shallow water, hit their head, or have other injuries (WMS, MedlinePlus). If one is possible, keep the head and neck stable and in line with the body as much as possible (MedlinePlus).

The side position is the Recovery position protocol.

steps.text: Take off wet clothing, dry them, and cover them to keep warm. If they are cold, use the Hypothermia protocol.
steps.detail: Remove cold, wet clothing and cover them with something warm to prevent hypothermia (MedlinePlus). After cold water, handle them gently and keep them lying down if they are drowsy or confused (Hypothermia protocol).

steps.text: Did they need rescue breaths or CPR, or were they unresponsive at any time?
steps.detail: MedlinePlus: anyone who needed any resuscitation, even rescue breaths alone, should go to hospital, even if they now seem alert with good breathing.

ask.q: Did they need breaths or CPR, or were they unresponsive?

steps.text: Do they have any trouble breathing, a bad or worsening cough, foam at the mouth, or are they drowsy or confused?
steps.detail: WMS 2024: evacuate immediately for abnormal breathing sounds, a severe cough, frothy or foamy fluid from the airway, reduced alertness, or low blood pressure (faint, pale, weak pulse).

ask.q: Any breathing trouble, bad cough, foam, or drowsiness?

steps.text: No symptoms, or only a mild cough: someone stays with them and watches them closely for 6 hours. Evacuate if breathing trouble, a worse cough or drowsiness develops.
steps.detail:
WMS 2024 (wilderness): someone with no symptoms apart from a mild cough may be released, ideally with someone staying with them for 6 hours, or told to get help if symptoms develop. If evacuation is difficult, watch people with mild symptoms and normal alertness for 6 hours; evacuate promptly if they get worse. A mildly affected person who has had no symptoms for 6 hours may not need evacuation.

WMS also requires normal breath sounds through a stethoscope before release; most groups cannot check this, so watch closely.

MedlinePlus: lung problems are common after drowning, even when the person seems fine at the scene.

steps.text: Evacuate now. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Keep them warm, watch their breathing, and be ready to start CPR.
steps.detail:
Lung problems, heart rhythm problems and other injuries can develop after drowning, even if the person seems well (MedlinePlus).

Oxygen: if your group carries oxygen and someone trained to give it is there, give it. WMS 2024: give oxygen at the highest concentration available. AHA 2025 (Class 1): trained rescuers should give supplemental oxygen, if available, after cardiac arrest from drowning.

If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR with rescue breaths (use the CPR, adult protocol (or CPR, child or CPR, infant)).

donts: Do not go into the water, onto ice, or into rough water to rescue someone unless you are trained.
Do not try chest compressions in the water.
Do not push on the belly or do abdominal thrusts to get water out.
Do not put on an AED before starting CPR with breaths.
Do not let someone who was rescued from the water go off alone, even if they seem fine.
evacuate: Evacuate urgently: anyone who needed rescue breaths or CPR, or was unresponsive at any time (MedlinePlus).
Evacuate urgently: trouble breathing, a severe cough, frothy fluid from the mouth, drowsiness or confusion, or faintness (WMS).
Watch for 6 hours, with someone staying with them: no symptoms or only a mild cough (WMS). Evacuate if anything gets worse.
Evacuate: hypothermia (Hypothermia protocol) or other injuries.
